# Results — Study 274 (Fine-Wine) on the Liv-ex 100 vs S&P 500

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The Liv-ex 100
Fine Wine Index year-end levels are hardcoded in [`data.py`](../fine_wine/data.py)
(2003–2025). S&P 500 calendar-year price returns are from the repo-level
`_cache/^GSPC_split_only.parquet` (daily ^GSPC, December/December). Match the
fingerprint below to confirm you hold the same data. As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n observations | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| Liv-ex 100 (December level, base 100 = Jul-2001) | 2003–2025 | 23 levels → 22 annual returns | hardcoded constant |
| S&P 500 (^GSPC nominal price, Dec/Dec) | 2004–2025 | 22 years | `4d28cad3df77` |
| Merged (wine ∩ equity, calendar year) | 2004–2025 | 22 years | `4d28cad3df77` |

## Risk and return — wine *lags*

| Asset | CAGR | Annual vol (raw) | Annual vol (de-smoothed) | Sharpe (rf 2%) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Liv-ex 100 (price, mid-price) | **4.7%** | 14.1% | **19.4%** | **0.25** |
| S&P 500 (price-only) | **8.6%** | 16.3% | — | **0.49** |

The fine-wine index returned **4.7%/yr** versus the S&P 500's **8.6%/yr** over
2004–2025 — wine lagged equities by ~3.9pp/yr, *before* the very large frictions
wine carries. Both series are **price-only**: the S&P figure excludes dividends
(a ~1.8pp/yr understatement of equity total return), and the Liv-ex 100 is a
mid-price index that pays no income while costing storage and insurance. On a
total-return basis the gap is wider, not narrower.

## Correlation — low on paper, higher once de-smoothed

| Measure | Value |
|---|--:|
| Raw correlation (Liv-ex 100 vs S&P 500, annual) | **+0.10** |
| Liv-ex 100 first-order autocorrelation (smoothing ρ) | **+0.31** |
| **De-smoothed (Geltner) correlation** | **+0.28** |

The headline the wine-merchants quote is the **+0.10** raw correlation — and at
face value that is a near-perfect diversifier. But the Liv-ex 100 is a
**mid-price** index: each component is marked at the average of the live bid and
offer, which **smooths** the series. The smoothing shows up as a +0.31
first-order autocorrelation in annual returns. Applying the standard Geltner
(1991/1993) first-order unsmoothing recovers an underlying series with **~19.4%
volatility** (vs 14.1% reported) and a correlation with equities of **+0.28** —
nearly triple the raw number. The low correlation is real but **partly an
artefact of appraisal smoothing**, exactly as Geltner predicts for illiquid,
mark-to-model indices.

## The diversification-benefit test (20% wine sleeve)

Does adding a 20% wine sleeve to a 100%-equity book raise the Sharpe ratio? Four
lenses, from most flattering to most honest:

| Lens | Blend Sharpe | vs equity-only (0.490) | HAC t on benefit |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Gross / raw (reported returns, no costs) | **0.522** | **+0.032** | −0.82 |
| Net / raw (storage + rebalancing costs) | 0.477 | −0.013 | — |
| Gross / de-smoothed (honest risk) | 0.484 | −0.006 | — |
| **Net / de-smoothed (the only honest number)** | **0.442** | **−0.047** | **−1.35** |

- On the **gross/raw** lens the blend's Sharpe edges up (+0.032) — this is the
  marketing number, and even here the Newey-West HAC t-stat on the per-year
  benefit is **−0.82** (not positive, let alone significant).
- Charge wine's real frictions (a one-way spread of ~10% on rebalanced notional
  plus ~1%/yr storage/insurance) and the benefit **disappears**.
- De-smooth the risk *and* charge costs — the only defensible accounting — and
  the blend Sharpe **falls below** equity-only by **−0.047**, with a HAC
  t-stat of **−1.35**. There is no robust diversification benefit.

## Positive control

On a synthetic tape (`synthetic_annual`) with a planted **zero** true
correlation and **smooth = 0.5**, the machinery reproduces the trap: the
*measured* correlation reads near zero while the de-smoothing correctly recovers
the true near-zero underlying — and with a planted **+0.5** true correlation and
smoothing, de-smoothing recovers the higher number that the raw series hides.
The engine detects diversification benefit when one is planted (positive HAC t),
and reports none when none exists. The real Liv-ex tape lands in the "no robust
benefit" bucket.

## The n = 22 problem

With only 22 annual observations, a correlation of 0.28 has a 95% CI of roughly
[−0.15, 0.62]; the Sharpe-improvement HAC t-stats are all well inside ±2. Fine
wine *might* be a genuine low-correlation asset, but this sample cannot resolve a
diversification benefit, and the point estimates (net of honest costs and risk)
are **negative**.

## Could you trade it?

There is no liquid, low-cost vehicle. You buy physical cases or via a merchant
at the offer, sell at the bid, and the Liv-ex round-trip spread is on the order
of 10–15%; storage and insurance run ~£10–15/case/year; settlement takes weeks.
The index itself is **uninvestable** — it is a mid-price benchmark, not a fund.
Wine funds that tried to track it have largely closed or underperformed after
fees. The honest conclusion: wine is a *mild* diversifier on paper that
**lags equities, de-smooths to a higher beta, and is eaten alive by frictions**.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The low raw correlation (+0.10) is real but inflated by
  appraisal smoothing; de-smoothed it is **+0.28**, a modest-but-nonzero equity
  beta with genuine literature support (wine *does* diversify a little). It is
  **not** the clean zero-correlation diversifier of the sales pitch, and no
  diversification-benefit HAC t-stat reaches +2 (best is −0.82). Real-ish,
  weak, and confounded.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Wine lags equities by ~3.9pp/yr; the index is a
  mid-price benchmark with no investable vehicle; round-trip spreads of ~10–15%
  plus storage erase any paper benefit. Net of de-smoothed risk and costs the
  20% sleeve **lowers** the portfolio Sharpe (−0.047).
